questions.q: What does this lesson say about treating build-vs-buy as an ideological, always-the-same-answer choice?
options: It is the correct approach, since consistency matters more than case-by-case analysis
Buying is always correct for middleware decisions specifically
It is itself a mistake an architect should push back on; there is no universal right answer, and the decision should be evaluated case by case using specific factors
Building is always correct for middleware decisions specifically
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues against a one-size-fits-all rule in either direction — build-vs-buy is a genuine trade-off analysis that should be evaluated case by case against the specific factors listed, not decided ideologically.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say comparing subscription cost against zero is a flawed way to evaluate build vs. buy?
options: Because building in-house isn't free — it costs developer time to build and ongoing developer time to maintain indefinitely, so a fair comparison uses total cost of ownership over several years for both options
Because subscription cost is always lower than building, so the comparison is unnecessary
Because buy decisions never have any ongoing cost after the first year
Because build decisions never require any ongoing maintenance
questions.explain: A fair build-vs-buy comparison has to account for the fully-loaded cost of building and maintaining custom infrastructure over time (total cost of ownership), not just compare a subscription's sticker price against an assumed-free in-house alternative.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which kind of integration need tilts the decision toward "buy"?
options: A need that's genuinely unique to one specific business, with no existing vendor connector anywhere
A need with no urgency and no deadline pressure at all
A need involving highly unusual data residency rules a vendor platform cannot accommodate
A need that's common across many companies, which a mature iPaaS vendor has likely already built a pre-packaged connector for
questions.explain: A common, widely-shared integration need (connecting to a major ERP or marketing platform) is exactly what vendors have already built pre-packaged connectors for, capturing work already done once and sold to many customers — tilting the decision toward buy.

questions.q: What risk does "key-person dependency" describe in the context of a build decision?
options: The risk that a vendor's pricing increases unexpectedly
The risk that a custom-built system becomes unmaintainable if the one person who deeply understands it leaves the organization
The risk that an iPaaS platform is discontinued by its vendor
The risk that an API version is deprecated without notice
questions.explain: Key-person dependency is specifically a build-decision risk: a custom system that only one developer deeply understands becomes fragile and hard to maintain the moment that person is no longer available.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked TCO example, why does the conclusion change if the company's actual integration need turns out to be genuinely unique rather than standard?
options: It wouldn't change at all; TCO numbers are independent of how standard the need is
Because unique needs always cost less to build than standard ones
Because if no vendor connector exists for a unique need, the "buy" option wouldn't actually solve the problem out of the box, so the pure TCO comparison alone is insufficient to justify buying
Because standard needs can never be solved by a build decision
questions.explain: The worked example notes that TCO numbers favoring buy only fully apply when the standardness factor also points toward buy (a pre-built connector exists); for a genuinely unique need with no vendor connector, buying wouldn't solve the problem regardless of what the raw cost comparison shows.
